```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(CalTools)
```

CalTools 0.2.1 provides bounded calibration, explicit inconsistency diagnostics,
feasibility checks, directional bound relaxation and auditable margin aggregation.
All public identifiers, examples, messages, code comments and documentation are
in English. **Version 0.2.0 changes the public API**; see
[the migration guide](inst/doc/MIGRATION.md) before updating existing scripts.

## Installation and help

R >= 4.1.0 is required. Runtime dependencies are `lpSolve` and `quadprog`.
There is no package-specific C++ compilation and no external `sourceCpp()` path.

```{r installation, eval=FALSE}
install.packages(c("lpSolve", "quadprog"))
install.packages("CalTools_0.2.1.tar.gz", repos = NULL, type = "source")
library(CalTools)
?calibrate_weights
?analyze_inconsistency
?calibration_preflight
example("calibrate_weights", package = "CalTools")
```

The project includes roxygen2 source comments and generated `man/*.Rd` help files.
The help pages work immediately after installation; users do not need roxygen2.
Developers can run `roxygen2::roxygenise("CalTools")` to regenerate them.
The maintainer email in `DESCRIPTION` is a declared placeholder; replace it
before publication. See [PUBLISHING.md](PUBLISHING.md).

## 1. Calibration and distance choices

For an $n\times p$ matrix $X$ and a vector of known totals $t$, calibration seeks
weights $w$ satisfying $X^\top w=t$. Quadratic calibration minimizes

$$Q(w)=\frac12\sum_i\frac{(w_i-d_i)^2}{s_iq_i},\qquad s_i>0,\ q_i>0.$$

Here `d` contains starting weights, `q` contains distance factors and
`metric_scale` represents $s$. The default $s_i=d_i$ requires positive initial
weights and gives the usual chi-square calibration distance. Setting
`metric_scale=1` selects a different, weighted Euclidean distance.

```{r data}
X <- cbind(
  group_A = c(rep(1, 5), rep(0, 5)),
  group_B = c(rep(0, 5), rep(1, 5)),
  age = 1:10
)
totals <- c(group_A = 24, group_B = 26, age = 290)
d <- rep(5, 10)
q <- rep(1, 10)
```

```{r calibration}
linear_fit <- calibrate_weights(X, d, totals)
bounded_fit <- calibrate_weights(X, d, totals, method = "truncated",
  lower = rep(1, 10), upper = c(rep(9, 9), 10))
raking_fit <- calibrate_weights(X, d, totals, method = "raking")
logit_fit <- calibrate_weights(X, d, totals, method = "logit",
  lower = seq(0, 1, length.out = 10), upper = seq(9, 12, length.out = 10))
bounded_fit
crossprod(X, bounded_fit$weights)
```

`lower` and `upper` always bound **final weights**, not multiplicative factors.
Both scalar and observation-specific vector bounds are accepted.

| Method | Domain and implementation |
|---|---|
| `linear` | Analytic quadratic solution in a reduced constraint space. |
| `truncated` | Convex quadratic calibration with reversible bound activity. `solver="dual"` uses the reduced dual; `solver="qp"` uses a reference QP; `auto` may use the QP fallback for at most 2000 rows. |
| `raking` | Entropic distance with positive starting weights; uses the full derivative including variable `q`. |
| `logit` | Finite vector bounds strictly enclosing positive starting weights; stable logistic formulas. |

Raking and logit do not accept `metric_scale`. Their multiplier algorithms seek
interior solutions; boundary-only targets may require `truncated` instead.
Nonconvergence is an error, not proof of infeasibility.

```{r distance}
calibration_distance(bounded_fit$weights, d, method = "truncated",
                     lower = 1, upper = c(rep(9, 9), 10))
calibration_distance_from_factors(bounded_fit$g, d, method = "truncated",
                                lower = 1, upper = c(rep(9, 9), 10))
linear_multipliers(X, d, totals)
calibrate(X, d, totals, description = TRUE)  # Short wrapper with the same fit object
```

Fit objects contain weights, factors `g`, multipliers `lambda`, objective,
residuals, numerical rank and solver details. Distances from different methods
are not comparable measures of statistical performance. Multipliers need not be
unique when columns are dependent.

## 2. Negative totals are supported

Negative totals do **not** require negative initial weights. For example, an
auxiliary variable can take negative values while all survey weights are positive.
The residual check is

$$\max_j\frac{|(X^\top w-t)_j|}{\max(1,|t_j|)}\le\texttt{tol}.$$

It uses the absolute magnitude of each total and remains defined at zero.

```{r negative-totals}
X_signed <- cbind(N = rep(1, 5), signed = -1:-5,
                  contrast = c(-2, -1, 0, 1, 2))
target_weights <- c(1, 2, 3, 2, 1)
signed_totals <- setNames(as.numeric(crossprod(X_signed, target_weights)),
                         colnames(X_signed))
signed_totals
signed_fit <- calibrate_weights(X_signed, rep(2, 5), signed_totals,
  q = c(.4, .8, 1, 1.3, 2), method = "truncated",
  lower = c(.1, .2, .3, .4, .5), upper = c(4, 5, 6, 5, 4))
signed_fit$residuals
```

The test suite also flips the signs of a column and its total together, and
checks that the fitted weights do not change. An impossible negative total
with a nonnegative column and nonnegative weight bounds is correctly rejected.

## 3. Negative or zero starting weights require an explicit metric

This is a different issue from negative totals. Using a negative starting weight
as a quadratic denominator can destroy convexity. Select a positive scale explicitly.

```{r signed-weights}
X_small <- cbind(N = 1, x = 1:4)
starting_weights <- c(-1, 0, 2, 3)
fit <- calibrate_weights(X_small, starting_weights, c(N = 8, x = 22),
  method = "truncated", lower = 0, upper = 5, metric_scale = 1)
fit$weights
fit$g  # NA where the starting weight is zero
```

Use `$weights` when a starting weight is zero. If factor bounds are converted
for negative `d`, their order reverses: use `pmin(lower_factor*d,upper_factor*d)`
and `pmax(lower_factor*d,upper_factor*d)`. Positive factor bounds preserve the
sign of `d`; use final-weight bounds when negative weights must become positive.

## 4. Find and explain incompatible totals

The system is consistent precisely when appending $t^\top$ to $X$ does not
increase its row-space rank. Equivalently, every relation $Xc=0$ must satisfy
$c^\top t=0$. The numerical implementation scales columns, computes an SVD and
checks the new row against the resulting row space.

```{r incompatibilities}
X_conflict <- cbind(group_A = c(1, 0), group_B = c(0, 1), N = c(1, 1))
conflicting_totals <- c(group_A = 4, group_B = 6, N = 11)
analyze_inconsistency(X_conflict, conflicting_totals)
report <- analyze_inconsistency(X_conflict, conflicting_totals, details = TRUE)
report
report$incompatibilities
report$coefficients
```

`details=FALSE` preserves a simple logical result. `details=TRUE` reports:

- `rank_X` and `rank_augmented`, using the stated numerical tolerances;
- `relations` and their numerical coefficient matrix;
- `incompatibilities`: violated relations, discrepancies, thresholds and involved margins;
- `projected_totals` and `residuals`, for diagnosis only.

The example exposes the conflict between `group_A + group_B` and `N`.
It does not decide which source total is incorrect. The relation set is not
promised to be minimal or independent. Input totals are never changed.
`rank_tol` determines numerical rank; `tol` determines admissible discrepancies
in the original total units. Near numerical dependence, both settings matter.

```{r structural-diagnostics}
X_redundant <- cbind(X, N = X[, "group_A"] + X[, "group_B"], empty = 0)
analyze_collinearity(X_redundant, simple = TRUE)
analyze_zero_sample(X_redundant)
```

Redundancy alone is harmless if totals satisfy the same relations. A zero column
with a nonzero total is inconsistent. The zero-sample diagnostic uses an absolute
threshold; it never removes constraints.


### Nearest algebraically consistent totals

`analyze_inconsistency(..., details = TRUE)$projected_totals` is a diagnostic
computed after **column normalization**. To get the genuinely nearest vector
in the **original total units**, use `closest_consistent_totals()`:

```{r closest-totals}
X_conflict <- cbind(group_A = c(1, 0), group_B = c(0, 1), N = c(1, 1))
conflicting_totals <- c(group_A = 4, group_B = 6, N = 11)
closest_consistent_totals(X_conflict, conflicting_totals)
# group_A = 4.333333, group_B = 6.333333, N = 10.666667
closest_consistent_totals(X_conflict, conflicting_totals,
                          scales = c(1, 1, 10), details = TRUE)
```

It minimizes `sum(((t_star - totals)/scales)^2)/2`, subject to the existence of
**some** (possibly unbounded or negative) `w` with `crossprod(X,w)=t_star`.
The optional `scales` control which totals are trusted most; larger values
permit larger changes. **This does not ensure bounded-weight feasibility.**
Check the adjusted vector again with `calibration_preflight()` if needed.

## 5. Initial screening and bounded feasibility

```{r preflight}
calibration_preflight(X_conflict, conflicting_totals, lower = 0, upper = 10)
consistent_totals <- c(group_A = 4, group_B = 6, N = 10)
calibration_preflight(X_conflict, consistent_totals, lower = 0, upper = 3)
calibration_preflight(X_conflict, consistent_totals, lower = 0, upper = 10)
```

The statuses separate `inconsistent_totals`, `bound_infeasible`, `feasible` and
`numerical_failure`. Moving bounds cannot repair incompatible equalities.
Preflight and bounded feasibility require finite bounds.

```{r feasibility}
check <- calibration_feasibility(X, totals, lower = 1, upper = 10)
check[c("feasible", "status", "solver", "max_scaled_residual")]
calibration_feasibility(X, totals, 1, 10, method = "lp")$feasible
is_feasible(X, totals, lower = 1, upper = 10)
is_feasible_fast(X, totals, lower = 1, upper = 10)
is_feasible_lp(X, totals, lower = 1, upper = 10)
```

`TRUE` includes a checked witness. `FALSE` comes from an inconsistent equality
system, a box-support certificate, or the LP solver's infeasible status.
`NA` means inconclusive. Boolean wrappers raise an error on an inconclusive result.
The LP uses $w=L+z$, with $z\ge0$, and sparse constraint triplets.
`is_feasible_fast` shares the validated default implementation with `is_feasible`.

## 6. Projection algorithms: scope and limitations

For the affine set $C=\{w:X^\top w=t\}$ and the box $B=[L,U]$, ordinary alternating
projections iterate $w^{k+1}=P_B(P_C(w^k))$. They allow bound activity to change.

```{r projection}
projection_check <- calibration_feasibility(X, totals, 1, 10,
  method = "projection", max_iter = 5000, fallback = FALSE)
projection_check[c("feasible", "status", "solver", "max_scaled_residual")]
```

The affine projection reuses an orthonormal basis. Its per-iteration cost is
$O(nr)$ after reduction, where $r$ is the constraint rank. With `fallback=FALSE`,
iteration exhaustion returns `NA`, not `FALSE`; with `fallback=TRUE`, it runs the LP.
`method="auto"` remains the quadratic dual with LP fallback, not ordinary
alternating projections. Ordinary alternating projections are used here only to
find a feasible witness, not to claim the closest calibrated weights.

The original permanent-clipping procedure is different: it could fix an incorrect
face and report infeasibility. A four-unit counterexample and the full explanation
are in [MATHEMATICS.md](inst/doc/MATHEMATICS.md).

Projection-based feasibility and best approximation are established subjects:
Bauschke and Borwein (1996), and Boyle and Dykstra (1986), provide key references.
Devaud and Tille (2019, Section 3.2.2) discuss closely related reduced Newton
calibration, singularity at tight bounds and a more expensive general alternative.
This supports the computational motivation, not the correctness of irreversible
clipping. Farkas' lemma is a theorem of alternatives, not a competing runtime
algorithm. Comparisons depend on the particular LP formulation and solver.
See [PROJECTIONS_AND_LITERATURE.md](inst/doc/PROJECTIONS_AND_LITERATURE.md).

## 7. Relax bounds along a declared direction

`relax_bounds` minimizes $\rho\ge0$ subject to calibration and
$L_i-\rho a_i\le w_i\le U_i+\rho b_i$. The rates are nonnegative scalar or vector
arguments. This is the minimal expansion along that direction, not the nearest
box under every possible metric.

```{r bound-relaxation}
relax_bounds(matrix(1, 3, 1), 9, 0, 2, lower_rate = 0, upper_rate = 1)
analyze_feasibility_bounds(X, totals, d, type = "g-weight", method = "upper",
  bounds = c(.9, 1.1), search_limits = 2, step = .1)
analyze_feasibility_bounds(matrix(1, 2, 1), 1, c(10, 20),
  type = "w-weight", method = "lower", bounds = c(1, 2), search_limits = 0, step = .25)
```

The grid interface uses binary search on nested boxes. `both` expands the two
endpoints simultaneously until their respective search limits. It is not an
exhaustive search over all endpoint pairs. The final endpoint is always included.
`g-weight` endpoints multiply starting weights; `w-weight` endpoints are absolute.

## 8. Modify margins explicitly

```{r margins}
merged <- merge_margins(X, totals, c("group_A", "group_B"), "N")
merged$totals
drop_margins(X, totals, "age")$totals
check_modified_feasibility(X, totals, d, lower = 4.5, upper = 5.5,
  margin_names = c("group_A", "group_B"), action = "join", merged_name = "N",
  bounds = c(.9, 1.1), search_limits = 2, step = .1)
check_sequential_feasibility(X, totals, d, lower = 4.5, upper = 5.5,
  margin_names_list = list(c("group_A", "group_B"), "age"),
  actions = c("join", "suppress"), merged_names = list("N", NULL),
  bounds = c(.9, 1.1), search_limits = 2, step = .1)
```

Merging sums columns and totals; dropping removes equations. Both weaken the
constraints and do not guarantee the original separate totals. Names and their
order must match. Zero-column matrices are supported. The sequential function
returns the first feasible result, or the last attempted problem with its history.
These checks try the supplied vector bounds first; their common-bound grid can
replace that box. Use directional relaxation instead if individual limits must
retain their substantive meaning.

## 9. Automatic and interactive workflows

```{r recommendations}
margin_groups <- list(c("group_A", "group_B"))
recommend_margin_merges(X, d, totals, margin_groups = margin_groups,
                       ordered = FALSE, criterion = "sample")
recommend_margin_merges(X, d, totals, margin_groups = margin_groups,
                       ordered = FALSE, criterion = "lambda")
adjacent_elements(c("young", "middle", "older"), 2)
```

Recommendations are heuristics. Multiplier scores are scaled by column norms but
still depend on a representation when columns are dependent. Groups must be
disjoint. `ordered=TRUE` permits only adjacent pair merges within a linear order.

```{r automatic}
X_search <- diag(3)
colnames(X_search) <- c("A", "B", "C")
search_totals <- c(A = 0, B = 0, C = 6)
candidates <- automatic_calibration(X_search, search_totals, rep(1, 3),
  lower = 1, upper = 3, bounds = c(1, 3), search_limits = c(1, 3),
  margin_groups = list(c("A", "B", "C")), ordered = TRUE,
  max_depth = 2, max_solutions = 3)
candidates
attr(candidates, "preflight")
candidates[[1]]$history
candidates[[1]]$residuals_original
```

The breadth-first search updates groups and deduplicates equivalent partitions.
It stops at the requested solution, depth or node limits. Every candidate includes
the actual matrix, totals, bounds, weights, history and original residuals.
It never deletes a nonzero population total silently.

```{r conflicting-workflow}
X_inconsistent <- cbind(A = c(1, 0), B = c(2, 0))
bad_totals <- c(A = 2, B = 5)
stopped <- automatic_calibration(X_inconsistent, bad_totals, c(1, 1),
  lower = 0, upper = 10, margin_groups = list(c("A", "B")), ordered = TRUE)
stopped  # No bound search or fitting: the original equalities conflict.
# Explicitly permit changing the equalities through aggregation:
merged_candidates <- automatic_calibration(X_inconsistent, bad_totals, c(1, 1),
  lower = 0, upper = 10, margin_groups = list(c("A", "B")), ordered = TRUE,
  on_inconsistency = "merge")
merged_candidates[[1]]$residuals_original
```

`on_inconsistency="stop"` is the default. It returns an empty search with the
initial diagnostic, so you can inspect the conflict before editing anything.
`"merge"` allows weakened problems, not a claim that the original conflict vanished.
At every search node, inconsistent equalities skip the bound-relaxation stage.

```{r interactive}
selected <- interactive_calibration(X_search, search_totals, rep(1, 3),
  lower = 1, upper = 3, margin_groups = list(c("A", "B", "C")), ordered = TRUE,
  bounds = c(1, 3), search_limits = c(1, 3),
  choose = function(candidates) 1L)
selected$fit
selected$preflight$status
```

In an interactive R console, omit `choose` to see the initial diagnostic and
choose a candidate; zero cancels. In scripts provide `choose`. No candidates
returns an empty search with diagnostics; cancellation returns `NULL`.

## 10. Random inclusion probabilities

```{r probabilities}
set.seed(12)
probabilities <- random_inclusion_probabilities(N = 100, n = 10)
c(sum = sum(probabilities), minimum = min(probabilities), maximum = max(probabilities))
```

The generator normalizes exponential sizes with certainty units. It returns
values in $[0,1]$ summing to `n`, including the endpoints `n=0` and `n=N`.
It is not uniform on the fixed-sum polytope and does not reproduce the old
beta-rejection distribution.


### Reproducible random calibration stress tests

The generator constructs categorical partitions (complete sets of dummy
variables), binary, signed and positive numeric variables, zero-sample margins
and exactly dependent columns. It returns the `X`, `totals`, `d`, `q`, vector
bounds and `margin_groups` accepted directly by the current public API.

```{r random-stress-tests, eval=FALSE}
feasible_case <- generate_calibration_problem(
  n = 30, categorical_groups = c(5, 4), n_binary = 2, n_continuous = 1,
  n_zero = 1, n_derived = 1, difficulty = .25, seed = 42)
calibration_preflight(feasible_case$X, feasible_case$totals,
                      feasible_case$lower, feasible_case$upper)$status
# "feasible"

hard_case <- generate_calibration_problem(
  n = 30, categorical_groups = c(5, 4), n_binary = 2,
  difficulty = .8, stress_pattern = "local", seed = 42)
calibration_preflight(hard_case$X, hard_case$totals,
                      hard_case$lower, hard_case$upper)$status
# "bound_infeasible"

# Use the same generated object in the new automatic workflow.
candidates <- automatic_calibration(hard_case$X, hard_case$totals,
  hard_case$d, q = hard_case$q,
  lower = hard_case$lower, upper = hard_case$upper,
  bounds = hard_case$bounds, method = "upper", search_limits = 3,
  step = .1, margin_groups = hard_case$margin_groups,
  ordered = hard_case$ordered, max_solutions = 3, max_depth = 2)

bad_case <- generate_calibration_problem(
  n = 30, categorical_groups = c(5, 4), inconsistency = "linear", seed = 42)
analyze_inconsistency(bad_case$X, bad_case$totals)
# TRUE
closest_consistent_totals(bad_case$X, bad_case$totals)
```

**Operational difficulty:** for `difficulty <= 0.5`, a known solution meets
all initial bounds; for `difficulty > 0.5`, the totals violate the box support
of at least one margin and require relaxing or weakening constraints. With
`stress_pattern="local"`, this targets a low-frequency category to exercise
aggregation strategies; with `"global"`, it stresses all observations and is
better for bound-expansion benchmarks. `max_excess` sets the maximum extra
excursion. The parameter does **not** prescribe a particular number of search
nodes or margin merges. `inconsistency="linear"` or `"zero"` independently
creates contradictory equations; these cannot be fixed by bounds alone.

Legacy-style fields `Xs`, `total`, `L_bounds`, `U_bounds`, `mar_2_join` and
`hierarchy` are available on the generated object, but the **package function
names** follow the 0.2.x migration (`automatic_calibration`,
`calibration_preflight`, `analyze_collinearity`, etc.). For repeated runs see
`inst/benchmarks/random-problems.R`.

## 11. Reproducibility and limits

Every public function has roxygen2 documentation and runnable help examples.
Tests cover analytic solutions, an independent QP reference, negative and zero
totals, sign invariance, rank diagnostics, preflight policies and search depth.

```{r development, eval=FALSE}
# From the directory containing the package project:
roxygen2::roxygenise("CalTools")
testthat::test_local("CalTools")
# After installing the current package:
rmarkdown::render("CalTools/README.Rmd")
# In a terminal:
# R CMD build CalTools
# R CMD check --no-manual CalTools_0.2.1.tar.gz
```

The numerical core is dense. Initial reduction costs about $O(np^2)$ for $n\ge p$.
A dual Newton iteration costs $O(nr^2+r^3)$; an alternating-projection iteration
costs $O(nr)$. Detailed relation reporting adds a $p\times p$ projector. The QP
fallback has quadratic memory in `n`, hence its 2000-row limit. Finite iteration
budgets are not universal convergence guarantees. Validation uses synthetic data;
no performance or statistical-efficiency claim is made for unseen survey data.
